title: the Ramayana in every language
hookLine: a grandmother tells the Ramayana in English; is it still the Ramayana?
carry: the Ramayana is meant to be retold
tomorrow: a monk lands in America with no address. who takes him in?

cards: Bedtime, two kids in a bunk bed, a grandmother on the edge of the lower one. She's telling how Hanuman leaped the sea to Lanka, in English, because English is the language these two dream in.
Halfway through she stops, hunting for a word. From the top bunk: the monkey army, Nani. She laughs and keeps going.
In the kitchen, an aunt shakes her head. In English, she says, it isn't the Ramayana anymore.

teach.h: AS LONG AS RIVERS FLOW, IT TRAVELS.
teach.b: Two views live inside the tradition here, and each has a strong case. First, the grandmother's.

In the Ramayana's own opening chapters, the god Brahma tells the poet Valmiki to sing Rama's story, and promises, in paraphrase: as long as mountains stand and rivers flow on the earth, the Ramayana will go on traveling among people.
Mountains and rivers are everywhere, a hill behind a suburb included. And the retellings didn't wait for English.
Tulsidas told Rama's story in the everyday language around him, and at the start of his Ramcharitmanas he says he wrote it for the joy of his own heart.
That's a real Hindu habit: the Ramayana is meant to be retold, and it has been, in language after language. It's the story many families tell at Diwali, when Rama comes home to Ayodhya.
A story that travels learns new words. Now the aunt's case, and it's a serious one. Sanskrit isn't only a vehicle for the plot.

teach.h: THE SOUND IS PART OF IT.
teach.b: For some families the sound itself matters, and verses are chanted in the original even by people who don't follow every word.
In the Ramayana itself, Rama's twin sons sing the poem aloud, and the listeners are moved by the singing. Lose the sound, the aunt would say, and the children get the story but miss the song.
Neither one wants the story to fade. One is protecting how far it can go. The other is protecting what it is.

how: Hindu families abroad tell the Ramayana in many home languages, and some also keep Sanskrit verses chanted in the original at home and in temples.

s: the Ramayana's own opening says the story will keep traveling among people
Brahma promises Valmiki: as long as mountains stand and rivers flow.
Rama's story was told only in Sanskrit until it reached the West
Tulsidas retold it in the everyday language around him, in his Ramcharitmanas.

for some families the sound itself matters, understood or not.

games.q: your cousin wants every wedding reading in English so the guests can follow. state the best case for the other side.
o: the sound of the original carries something a translation can flatten.
English readings are disrespectful to the elders, full stop.
nobody understands Sanskrit anyway, so it's only habit.
games.why: the best case for Sanskrit isn't snobbery: in the Ramayana itself the poem is sung aloud, and the singing moves the listeners. the sound is part of what's handed on.

practice: Let a voice come back that once told you a story aloud, any story, in any language. Don't retell it. Just listen inside for the voice: its pauses, the place it slowed down.
Stay with the sound of it for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The diaspora: Hindus far from India, carrying the old stories into new languages, and arguing, lovingly, about the old sounds.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the epic of Rama, credited to the poet Valmiki.
